quiz: Think about what the model actually outputs: text or a structured request. Something else must run it.
The model can only read the text you give it about each tool. Which field explains when to use the tool?
ReAct loops think, act, then look at what came back. What new information arrives after an action?
Step k resends all k earlier chunks. Add up 1 + 2 + ... + n and see how that total grows.
Small facts that must be exactly right need storage you can look up precisely, not fuzzy similarity.
MCP splits control three ways: tools, resources and prompts each have a different owner. Recall who picks tools.
Ask whether text from an outside page should ever be treated as a command or only as data.
Multiply the step reliability by itself 10 times: 0.95 to the power 10.
Multi-agent helps when work is wide and independent. Look for the case where the task is small or tightly linked.
An agent can reach the right end state in a bad way. Think about cost, safety and the path it took.
Rank actions by impact and how hard they are to undo. Look for one that is risky and irreversible.
A model can ignore instructions in its prompt. Where can limits be enforced so they cannot be skipped?
Separate two checks: is the shape of the call valid, and is the value true in the real world?
Running a task several times and requiring every run to pass tells you about consistency, not just luck.
interview: Cover the full loop: tool definitions sent, model returns a structured call, your code runs it, the result goes back.
Explain the thought, action, observation cycle and why fresh real results reduce guessing on multi-step tasks.
Mention few focused tools, clear verb names, descriptions saying when to use them, enums, and strict input types.
Contrast step-by-step flexibility with planning up front; say when each fits and mention replanning on failure.
Describe memory tiers: recent turns, rolling summary, exact profile facts, and searchable past episodes.
Explain the host, client, server setup and what tools, resources and prompts are, then cover trust and injection risks.
Say when work is wide or needs independent checking, then cover costs: tokens, latency, coordination and debugging.
List failure modes like loops, tool misuse, bad arguments and injection, and pair each with a concrete guard.
Cover a task set from real logs, sandboxed end-state checks, trajectory grading, repeat runs, and cost tracking.
Score actions by impact and reversibility, tier the approval, and reduce fatigue with batching and clear summaries.
Start from traces of failed runs, cluster failures by type, fix the biggest cluster, and add evals to stop regressions.
Treat the run as durable saved state with a tool call ledger and idempotency keys so it can resume safely.
Spot the missing observation truncation and repeat detection, and suggest limits, summaries and better query planning.
